en: The Śrī Dattabhāvasudhārasa Stotra: [I bow to] Dattātreya, who consists of supreme bliss, who is sung of in the Vedas, who is immeasurable,
who is meditated upon by yogis, who has removed his own fear, and who has assumed many bodies.

I perpetually salute him who is unapproachable by the wicked, whose victory is far-reaching, who is worshipped by gods, daityas, and sages, who is ever-humble, imperishable, and accessible through true devotion. || 1 ||
O Dattātreya, salutations to you, the Blessed One who effects the destruction of sins,
who removes poverty, quiets fear, and extends compassion;
who uplifts devotees, bestows auspiciousness, and spreads noble fame.
O Lord of Excellence, O Master of Prosperity, O You who go the good path, You cause all beings to run [toward You] and grant them the supreme boon.
I pay homage to the one who generates good fortune, the savior, the leader of the world, the one free from sorrow, the protector of those who take refuge, and the fulfiller of desires. || 3 ||
I constantly remember your feet, which destroy weariness and bestow happiness;
grant me that pure state of being which would swiftly ward off [all afflictions]. (4)
I bow to Datta, the ocean of compassion, the kinsman of the distressed who bestows all prosperity, the kinsman who grants all auspiciousness, and who swiftly purifies even a defiled mind. || 5 ||
May he who dwells within and without all beings, the son of Atri, the emperor of ascetics,
whose fame pervades the quarters of space, and who has conquered the Death that stalks his devotees— may he protect me.

He is the remover of the fear and suffering of disease, mental affliction, and poverty; he assumes many bodies for his own protection; he is the master of his own servants and sports in manifold ways; though the agent, he is also the non-agent, being self-dependent and the destroyer of enemies.
And he was the son of Anasūyā, who was Viṣṇu himself for the sake of protecting the future;
indeed, his virtues cannot be fully enumerated here by the Creator, even until the end of the kalpa, by those possessed of wisdom.
Since all sufferings neither remain here nor in the next world due to the rain of nectar from his side-long glances, he,
the Infinite One, bestows the supreme goal.
May he, whose abode is divine, remain within me.
Therefore, be gracious, O destroyer of the suffering of the daughter of Atri,
O sky-clad one who roams within your own mind!
This wicked inscription which has been written here by the Creator—
That most auspicious [deed] must be performed by you, O Creator.
Endowed with all auspiciousness and possessed of all sovereignty, when you, the Lord of All, are pleased, what is difficult for whom to obtain? Where [could it be]? 11.
O Lord, the radiance of the ruby-like nails of Your feet alone is sufficient for us to destroy the blinding darkness within our hearts and reveal pure knowledge. 12.
If you would but look upon me even once with a sidelong glance moistened by your own compassion,
I shall here become one who has achieved his life's purpose and a worthy vessel for your abiding presence.
Where am I, dull-witted and wretched, and where are you, the blessed and powerful Lord?
Nevertheless, through the penetration of your presence, I am fortunate by your very glance.
Although various sins have been committed by me, nevertheless, through your grace, I am purified; of this there is no doubt. (15)
Indeed, you purify people by your own divine play; grant me the hearing of that divine play,
for with my eyes fixed intently upon it, I shall listen.
And I purify myself exceedingly, O God. || 16 ||
I declare clearly before you that I am indeed a mass of faults;
my faults, O Lord, are as immeasurable as drops in a rain of dust.
I am the foremost among the wicked, while you are the leader of the compassionate;
it appears to me that there is no one else more deserving of pity than I. 18.
O Compassionate One, if even upon seeing me in such a state your mind does not melt, then what more can be said to you regarding my unseen suffering? (19)
O Dattātreya, ocean of compassion, you alone have created us all;
we, your most wretched sons, are incapable of protecting ourselves. (20)
Victory, victory to Datta, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods; victory, victory to Bhadra, the bestower of auspiciousness, the object of worship for those seeking prosperity!
Victory, victory to the Eternal One, who is to be known through stainless wisdom!
Victory, victory to the Truthful One, who is true to his promise and blameless! || 21 ||
If I were your son, you alone would be my father and mother;
O Mother, quickly sprinkle me with the nectar of your compassionate breast-milk.
O Source of the Universe, since you are the creator whose efficient and material causes are non-different from Īśa, I am not your son; O Datta, protect me from this! 23.
O my child, whether my words are well-spoken or ill-spoken, you must forgive both them and my offense; for indeed, I have no other refuge but you.
O Father, for me, a fool who has no other refuge, it is not at all fitting to neglect you, nor even to take account of my faults. (25)
O Lord, abode of the ocean of compassion, because of my ignorance and lack of discernment, faults arise at every step; what shall I do? 26.
Moreover, if I should fall into despondency because of my offenses, would even a mother on earth be angry with her child who has merely stepped on her foot? (27)
When a wretched child has fallen into her lap and is being beaten with her foot, does the mother abandon him? Oh, on the contrary, she comforts him! (28)
O Lord, if you do not console me, who am in such a state, alas!
what refuge can there be for me, so wretched, without you? (29)
Let not even this thought enter your mind: "This child is deceitful and seeks his own interest";
for in this world, hungry children remember their own mother. (30)
The life of two parents who have been separated depends on one or the other child;
you, however, have granted me both—let there be no cruelty toward me.
O Lord, I am not able to propitiate you with my hymn of praise;
even Brahmā and the others were struck with wonder there, so how could I, who am dull-witted, be capable of it? (32)
O Omniscient One, O Compassionate One, O You who cherish Your devotees, please accept these words spoken by me as a child, whether they be well-spoken or ill-spoken. (33)
"Those who have come to you for refuge have indeed attained their purpose;
reflecting on this in my mind, I have come to you for refuge. (34)
"Those devotees who are devoted to you and intent on you partake in your happiness"—in accordance with this scriptural injunction, O Giver, I have come to you for refuge. (35)
"The Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, bestows grace upon those devoted to him.
Reflecting thus again and again, I somehow sustain my life-breaths.
I am your devotee and dependent upon you; I offer my body, mind, and wealth unto you. Please show mercy toward me. (37)
I know no devotion toward you, nor do I know the method of worship;
I have performed no acts of charity or righteousness—grant me grace alone. (38)
The life of celibacy and other disciplines were not practiced by me, nor was the Veda studied according to the prescribed rules;
the state of a householder was not entered into according to the rite—be gracious to me for this. (39)
I have had no association with the virtuous, nor have I served the elders; I have not been granted the instruction of the scriptures—please, simply show me compassion. (40)
Even when dharma is known, I have no inclination toward it; even when adharma is known, I do not desist from it because of that.
I shall do exactly as I have been commanded by Śrīdattanātha, who resides within my heart. || 41 ||
May my action, service, movement, journey, memory, thought, praise, and speech always, in every way, belong only to you. (42)
"Your vow is not pleasing to me; it is certain that you shall perish.
O Śrīdatta, having brought back my consciousness, I sustain my life. (43)
O Lord, he who became [my father] through the gift of himself, saying "I am given by me to you"—that Śrīdatta, the son of Anasūyā and Atri, is my refuge. (44)
The Lord Śrīdatta gave to Kārtavīryārjuna both kinds of yogic perfection, including unimpeded movement; he is my refuge. 45.
May that Śrīdatta, the best of teachers, who imparted the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) to Alarka after first causing him to abandon all conceptual constructions, be my refuge. (46)
May that Śrīdatta be my refuge, who bestowed upon Yadava the knowledge—attained from twenty-four gurus—regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. 47.
And Śrīdatta, who is my refuge, sent to Alarka—the son of Madālasā and a jewel among men—the knowledge of the self preceded by yoga. (48)
He who gave a virtuous son to Āyurāja, who was devoted to the duty of service, and who grants the true goal—this Śrīdatta is my refuge. 49.
He who bestowed the sciences upon the Brahmin Viṣṇudatta for the benefit of the world, and he who partook of his funeral offerings—may that Śrīdatta be my refuge. (50)
To Rāmamātra Reṇukā, whom the omniscient Śrīdatta proclaimed as the one for whom the rule of following her husband in death applies—he is my refuge. 51.
Śrī Datta, who [taught] the entire daily ritual along with its roots to King Somakīrti as being conducive to liberation, is my refuge. (52)
Satisfied by his hymn of praise, Śrīdatta, my refuge, revealed his true form to that devotee who merely bore the name and was despondent. 53.
May Śrī Datta, who declared the conditions of the ages under the guise of the dialogue between Kali and Brahmā, and who attained perfection through the service of his guru, be my refuge. (54)
Having heard the curse of Durvāsas, he who is imperishable assumed various incarnations for the sake of Ambarīṣa;
that Śrīdatta is my refuge. 55.
He who, though unborn, descended in three forms as if to taste the milk of Anasūyā’s virtue—he, Śrīdatta, is my refuge. (56)
He who was born through devotion to the Brahmin lady Sumati at Pīṭhāpura—his son, the protector Śrīpāda, also known as Śrīdatta, is my refuge. || 57 ||
Śrī Datta revealed from the mouth of a Siddha the original installation of Mahābaleśvara; he is my refuge. 58.
Since even Caṇḍālī was liberated there at Gokarṇa, Śrīdatta, who dwelt for three years at that place consisting of Liṅgas and Tīrthas, is my refuge. 59.
In the city of the Kurus on the island of Kṛṣṇā, Śrīdatta—who rescued me from death along with my mother and my wicked son—is indeed my refuge. 60.
Another lord shall rule the kingdom in Kurupura, even as a washerman;
that Śrīdatta vanished from the sight of the ignorant—he is my refuge.
He who, having slain treacherous thieves and those who betrayed their own devotees, restored his devotee to life—that Śrīdatta is my refuge. 62.
In the city of Karañja, for the sake of accomplishing the Pradoṣa vow of Ambā, there was a son named Nṛhari; may that Śrīdatta be my refuge. (63)
Having become mute due to his vow, Śrīdatta later spoke the Vedas to his mother and, departing as a wandering mendicant, awakened her, saying, "He is my refuge."
That renunciant residing in Kāśī, who bestows the state of desirelessness and clarifies the Vedic dharma, Śrī Datta is my refuge. (65)
Having circumambulated the earth along with his disciples and having looked upon his mother, Śrīdatta—who is my refuge—removed the pain of the Brahmin’s trident. 66.
Having accepted Sāyaṇadeva as his disciple, he protected him.
And when he was terrified by the cruel Yavana, Śrīdatta became my refuge.

Although he himself is the very embodiment of the sacred ford (tīrtha), Śrīdatta— who is my refuge— instructed his own people thoroughly in the true Dharma and urged them toward pilgrimage to the holy sites.
Accompanied by his disciples, he stayed at Paryalī-kṣetra near Vaidyanātha;
there, Śrīdatta—who is my refuge—rescued me from delusion. (69)
Śrīdatta is my refuge—he who made the learned Vidvatsuta, though ignorant and censured by the world, into a wise man with his tongue restored. 70.
He who, while staying at Nṛsiṃhavāṭikā, gave a treasure to a poor brāhmaṇa who lived on vegetables—he, Śrīdatta, is my refuge. 71.
He who, in an instant, revealed the pilgrimage to the three sacred sites (Tristhalīyātrā) to his devotee and made that field a granter of boons—that Śrīdatta is my refuge. 72.
Having warded off the suffering of the hungry ghosts, he who, filled with devotion, gave his two sons to the Brāhmaṇī—he, Śrīdatta, the bestower of the goal, is my refuge. (73)
He who, having taught the truth to the mother of a dead son, restored her child to life—even while standing upon the wish-fulfilling tree—that Śrīdatta is my refuge. (74)
May that Śrīdatta, the forest-fire for the wildfire of poverty, who as a lord caused even a barren buffalo to be milked for the sake of alms, be my refuge. (75)
Requested by the king, he came and resided in the monastery at Gāṇagāpura;
Śrīdatta, the deliverer from the Brahmarākṣasa, is my refuge. (76)
Seated upon a palanquin and fully adorned, he who, as the destroyer of pride, revealed his universal form to one who reviled him—that Śrīdatta is my refuge. (77)
He who enlightened those two arrogant haters of Brahmins when they were brought before him by Trivikrama—that Śrīdatta is my refuge. (78)
Having spoken of the four Vedas, their branches, and their auxiliary sciences, that Lord Śrī Datta—who removes the pride of the Brahmins—is my refuge. (79)
Śrī Datta, whose scriptural revelation is for the lowly, gave [the knowledge] of seven births by crossing over the seven lines; He is my refuge. 80.
To Trivikrama, he spoke of the course of karma; then Śrīdatta, who grants knowledge, placed me—who was separated and fallen—under his protection.
To Trivikrama, who had been seized by a *rakṣasa*, Śrīdatta spoke of the greatness of the sacred ash and the upward liberation described by Vāmadeva; he said, "He is my refuge. (82)
The son of Gopīnātha was ill and died; his wife lamented for him, but the yogi Śrīdatta, who is my refuge, enlightened her. 83.
He who, in another form, proclaimed the duties of women in the form of a dialogue between the preceptor Agastya and a ṛṣi—that wise Śrīdatta is my refuge. (84)
Having instructed the widow in her duties and followed her in death, Śrīdatta—who bestowed the ashes from his eyes—restored the deceased Brahmin to life; he is my refuge. (85)
Śrīdatta, who is my refuge, spoke to Satyā regarding the grace (prasāda) that had been offered to the prostitute, which was accompanied by the greatness of the rudrākṣa beads. (86)
My preceptor, the illustrious Śrīdatta, my refuge, truly recounted to Satya the greatness of the Śatarudrīya, which restores life to the king of the dead.
Śrīdatta, who has declared the narrative of Kaca, which concerns women’s mantras, their unworthiness, and the granting of prosperity and good fortune, as well as the Soma-vow—he is my refuge. 88.
He who, having restrained the wicked nature of the brahmin woman, praised the supreme daily rite for the brahmin—he, Śrīdatta, is my refuge. (89)
May that Śrīdatta be my refuge, who, desiring to abandon transgression, spoke of the duties of a householder to a Brahmin for the sake of gradual liberation.
Śrīdatta, who fed four thousand perfected beings (siddhas) by means of food cooked once for three men, is my refuge. 91.

Śrīdatta, who bestows fruits upon his devotees, gave his two sons after instructing them in the service of the Aśvattha tree; he, who granted a son to an old barren woman through a painter, is my refuge. 92.
Having caused him to perform service with dry wood and thus leading him to the state of being that very tree, Śrīdatta removed the leprosy of the brahmin; he is my refuge. 93.
He who, having examined Sāyaṇadeva even with great difficulty, declared him to be devoted [to the Lord]—that Śrīdatta, who established the rules for service to the Guru, is my refuge. (94)
Śrī Datta, who explained to his devotee the pilgrimage to Kāśī that pleases Śiva along with its prescribed rites as ordained by Tvaṣṭṛ, is my refuge. (95)
He who proclaimed the infinite vow established by Kauṇḍinya’s dharma, and he who caused it to be performed—Śrīdatta is my refuge. (96)
On the day of the Śivarātri vow, he revealed that Śrīśaila to Taṃtukā by means of his yogic power; that Śrīdatta is my refuge. 97.
Śrī Datta is my refuge—he who, even after making himself known as the Absolute Truth, caused Nandiśarman to fall from his view by means of his own vision. 98.
Having shown himself in a dream as being within the Kalleśvara Liṅga to Narakesarin, Śrīdatta, my refuge, bestowed his grace upon him. 99.
Though he bears eight forms and dwells in eight villages, he is affectionate toward his devotees;
during the festival of Dīpāvalī, that Śrīdatta became my refuge. 100.
Even after cutting down unripe [trees], he who gave grain to a Śūdra in that field received a hundredfold return; that Śrīdatta is my refuge. (101)
He who revealed the eight sacred fords (tīrthas) at the site of Gāṇagāpura on the Bhīmarathī river for the sake of his devotees—that Śrīdatta is my refuge. 102.
From the moment he granted the boon previously given, Śrīdatta—who brought a torrent of pain from boils upon the kingdom and cast his gaze upon the Mleccha—is my refuge. 103.
He who, under the pretext of a pilgrimage to Śrīśaila, was established at Puṣpapīṭha as the bestower of boons, and who vanished in the Kali age—he, the venerable Datta, is my refuge. (104)
His sleep is in Mātṛpura; his seat (pīṭha) is on Sahyaśikhara;
his offering of water (arghya) is in the city called Kāśī; his alms-round (bhikṣā) is in Kolāpura;
his meal (bhuji) is in Pāñcāla; and his wonderful leaf-offering (patra) is in Viṭṭhalapura.
In the city of the Kurus, he was remembered as Gāndharva-yujirācamaḥ, not in a place near, but far away. || 105 ||
He whose face is like a stainless lotus, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, who has supreme dispassion as his consort, and who is in every way independent;
he is the most supremely pure one, holding a sacred water-pot in his hand.
He whose body is supremely beautiful was the son of Anasūyā and Atri.
Salutations to you, the bestower of all desired things; salutations to you, the ordainer;
salutations to you, the remover of the entire multitude of sins committed by all;
salutations to you, the knower of the gestures of all; salutations to you, the sustainer.
Salutations to you, the performer of all desired deeds and the remover of all suffering. || 107 ||
Homage, homage be to you, the destroyer of cities; homage, homage be to you, the destroyer of the asuras;
homage, homage be to you, the destroyer of the wicked.
To the one who has been given [as a gift], to the destroyer of the affliction of those devoted to him. || 108 ||
O Śrīdatta, Lord of Gods, be gracious to me; O Śrīdatta, Lord of All, be gracious to me.
Be gracious, O Lord of Yoga, grant me yoga.
Do not cause a separation from your devotion. || 109||
Śrīdatto is victorious here; I meditate incessantly upon Datta, for by Datta my heart has been purified—therefore, let there be constant salutation to you, Datta.
There is no higher refuge than Datta according to the Vedas; I am the servant of Datta.
O Śrīdatta, may supreme devotion be mine; O Datta, O Lord, be gracious! (110)
Thus ends the *Śrī Dattabhāvasudhārasa Stotra*, composed by the venerable ascetic Śrī Śrī Śrī Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī, the preeminent teacher among the wandering mendicants of the Paramahaṃsa order.
